response.query: How should the public API and kernel registry be shaped (compute_oob_conformity signature, adapter interfaces, fallbacks) and what backward-compatibility/migration guarantees will we promise for binary wheels?
response.answer: Public API will remain stable, with new features added via adapter interfaces. Binary wheels will maintain compatibility, but no formal backward-compatibility guarantees are provided. Fallbacks will be implemented for critical functions.

results.title: API and ABI backward compatibility guarantees - ROOT - ROOT Forum
results.content:
Title: API and ABI backward compatibility guarantees - ROOT - ROOT Forum
# API and ABI backward compatibility guarantees. Most libraries provide strong API and ABI backward compatibility guarantees: any program compiled against version 1.A is guaranteed to work with any version >1.A and <2.0. ROOT doesn’t seem to have any API or ABI backward compatibility guarantee. In ROOT 6.16, it is `int (double, int) const` while it is `int (double, int, int, int) const` in ROOT 6.18. This is an API breaking change since the type of the expression `&TH1::FindFirstBinAbove` has changed. This is also an obvious ABI breaking change (that could have been avoided by keeping a two-arguments overload). A more subtle example of an ABI breaking change is the defaulting of `TLine::TLine()`. This brings me to my question: **What are ROOT’s guarantees for API and ABI compatibility?** (Is this documented somewhere?) If there is any kind of guarantee, I need to report the above as bugs; otherwise, I guess I need to recompile any ROOT-dependent code every time the framework is updated (which would be a very good reason to limit the amount of such code to a minimum). Each time you change the ROOT version that you use, you must rebuild all your libraries and executables which depend on it. Eons ago, when I complained about it to Rene Brun (the founder of this project), I got the reply that it’s because “ROOT is not a set of libraries but a framework”. Maintaining an API and ABI compatible library is very expensive: any change needs to be validated against potentially breaking API or ABI compatibility. What ROOT guarantees are two compatibility elements:. Given HEP’s limited investment in software it seemed more beneficial for the community to relax the API/ABI compat requirements, enabling cheaper technical evolution and in general investment in other SW areas. Source compatibility for functions like `TH1::FirstBinAbove` is more than just being able to call it with the same arguments. `int (TH1::*f)(double, int) const = &TH1::FindFirstBinAbove;`. I agree this is a niche use case, but it demonstrates how adding function parameters always breaks the API. Yup, I’m aware but due to its niche-ness that’s not how we tend to define source-compatibility :slight_smile: Thanks for your understanding!

results.title: Thoughts on Backward and Forward Compatibility
results.content: # Thoughts on Backward and Forward Compatibility. Be backward compatible with all versions forever(Which there are a huge price and source of complexity) or maybe there is a middle ground approach we could take? Backward compatibility is only one part of the story the whole compatibility story is much more complex involving Forward compatibility, Isolation, Interfaces, and lots of subtle details. ## **Backward Compatibility**. Backward compatibility is easy to understand. There are basically a couple of different possible ways we have to deal with backward compatibility:. Provide Backward compatibility - Contract Migration: So Let's say your code runs on version 2 now and what you could do is have the API for version v1 in place and they just redirect and migrate the request from v1 to v2 on the fly ar runtime. Provide Backward compatibility - New Operations: So basically you would append-only and just add new operations when you need to change. Provide Backward compatibility - Multiple Deploys: You could have 2 different versions running side by side v1 and v2. ## **Forward Compatibility**. Now. What is forward compatibility? Well, this means we will be compatible with future changes. However, there are things we can do to make forward compatibility more doable like:. There are other things you could to increase forward compatibility. So should we just ignore forward compatibility? Internally: You don't need backward and forward compatibility at all - since microservice provides you greatly isolation and therefore freedom. Externally: Meaning your public contract(i.g rest API) you will really need to be backward compatible and forward as much as possible. However, if you are in a monolith or shared-application world them you really need backward/forward compatibility internally and external because the tables are really your APIs. So depending on where you are the backward/compatibility trade-off might have a completely different weight, priority, and impact. Public interfaces can manifest themselves in almost all forms of software like and not limited by:. When we consider SOA / Microservice contract we often just consider our beautiful contract project or our REST endpoints, however, if users config things in Tables or XML thats part of the contract since it is public.

results.title: Backward Compatibility
results.content: # Backward Compatibility. When new versions are released, we can't simply throw away old versions and ask everyone to upgrade. There's a need for new versions to interwork with older versions. This is what we mean by **backward compatibility**. Backward compatibility ensures that customers can continue to use current products and services without being forced to upgrade. In **hardware**, it's about pin compatibility so that old peripherals can interface with newer versions of the system hardware. In **software**, backward compatibility is defined for open or public interfaces of software components or products. The **API layer** needs to be backward compatible so that calling a newer version of the API doesn't require changes in client software.
